date_label: Documented span of the read letters: [Postmark 1 March 1880] ('the sweetest Violet in England', to her mother) to [Postmark 22 July 1881] (to Violet directly); the acquaintance evidently predates the first letter, which recalls 'your promise to have tea with me'.
summary: Wilde's attention to Violet Hunt, daughter of the painter Alfred William Hunt and the novelist Margaret Raine Hunt, runs through his 1880-81 letters to her mother - tea at the family's Campden Hill home, 'the sweetest Violet in England I think her, though you must not tell her so', a poem promised and then sent - and one direct letter of July 1881 thanking her for praising his Poems: 'You have made me very happy.' Later accounts carry a claim that Wilde proposed or came near proposing marriage; it appears nowhere in the letters and remains unverified.

sources.quote: Dear Mrs Hunt, I hope that you have not forgotten your promise to have tea with me tomorrow (Tuesday) at five o'clock, and that your Violet – the sweetest Violet in England I think her, though you must not tell her so – will come too.
sources.context: Wilde to Mrs Alfred Hunt (Margaret Raine Hunt, Violet's mother), [Postmark 1 March 1880], 13 Salisbury Street
sources.supports: The courtship-register compliment routed through her mother, with the request that Violet not be told; March 1880
sources.provenance: PDF pp. 113-114. The sentence breaks across the page-turn at 'the | sweetest'.

sources.quote: Dear Miss Violet Hunt, I thank you very much for your kind letter, and am infinitely delighted that you have thought my poems beautiful. … You have made me very happy. Believe me ever sincerely yours.
sources.context: Wilde to Violet Hunt, [Postmark 22 July 1881], Keats House, Tite Street; signed Oscar Wilde - the only letter to Violet herself in the Index of Recipients
sources.supports: Direct warm correspondence by July 1881, closing 'You have made me very happy'
sources.provenance: PDF p. 139. Elision drops the Slander/Ridicule/Envy sentence, his ranking of 'The Burden of Itys' and 'The Garden of Eros', and the Burne-Jones river outing; fuller text in long-form notes.

sources.quote: The second woman he seriously thought of marrying, at the beginning of the 1880s, was Violet Hunt … Wilde described her as ‘the sweetest violet in England.’ They had met in London when she was not yet seventeen. ‘I feel like a young conqueror,’ he said as they talked intensely together. ‘We will rule the world—you and I—you with your looks and I with my wits.’
sources.context: Ellmann on Wilde's marriage prospects before Constance Lloyd. Florence Balcombe was the first, Lillie Langtry 'scarcely as a potential wife'. Hunt's own account is in her autobiography The Flurried Years (1926), which Ellmann quotes on the same page.
sources.provenance: PDF p. 330 (2013 edition; no printed folios).
